p: The letter says Paul is a prisoner, but not where. Rome, Caesarea and Ephesus have all been suggested.
b: Paul calls himself a prisoner here, in 3:1 and in 6:20, where he adds that he wears "a chain." Acts tells of two long custodies: two years in Caesarea (Acts 24:27) and two years in Rome, where he "stayed on in quarters he paid for himself" (Acts 28:30). One view, if Paul wrote the letter, is Rome, about AD 62. Some scholars prefer Caesarea, and some propose an unrecorded jailing in Ephesus (compare 2 Corinthians 11:23). If Paul did not write the letter, the "prisoner" is a portrait of the apostle drawn by a follower who wanted his authority behind the words. Either way, the first readers were asked to take a prisoner's appeal seriously.
r: Ephesians 3:1; Ephesians 6:20; Acts 24:27; Acts 28:16; Acts 28:30; Philemon 1:9; 2 Corinthians 11:23

p: Paul's word for conduct is "walk": how a person's whole life moves along.
b: The Greek peripateo literally means to walk around. Paul uses it for a whole way of life, and Ephesians uses it again and again: how you once walked (2:2), the good works God prepared for us to walk in (2:10), and then here, in 4:17, 5:2, 5:8 and 5:15. The picture comes from the Hebrew Bible, where to "walk" (halak) with or before God means to live a life, and it is the root of the later Jewish word halakhah, the path of practice that a community follows. Romans uses the same idiom (Romans 6:4; Romans 13:13). This site keeps the word "walk" so the reader can follow the thread through the letter.

t: Humility was not a Greek virtue
p: The Greek word for "humble" usually meant low or servile before Christians used it as praise.
b: Greek writers generally used tapeinos for what is low, servile or shameful, and not as praise. Commentators point out that the Christian use, as in Philippians 2:3 and Colossians 3:12, turns the word around, with Jesus as the pattern (Matthew 11:29). In Ephesians the humility asked for is not self-hatred. It is the stance that lets people "put up with one another in love," the practical test of a church made of Jews and Gentiles, slaves and free, rich and poor, who would not normally have eaten at one table.

a: the unity that the Spirit gives
p: The unity is a gift of the Spirit that believers guard; they do not build it.
b: "Of the Spirit" can mean the unity the Spirit makes, or a oneness of spirit among people. The first fits better, since the next lines name "one Spirit" and the verb is "keep," which is what you do with something you already have. Chapter 2 has said that Christ made Jew and Gentile "one new humanity" (see 2:14-18); the task now is to protect what he made. The word "tie" (syndesmos) is not from the same word-family as the "joint" (haphe) of 4:16, but the two are set side by side in Colossians 2:19 ("joints and ligaments"), and the "bond" of Colossians 3:14 is the same word as the "tie" here: peace is the ligament that holds the body together.

a: There is one body and one Spirit
p: Seven "ones" follow a pattern: Spirit, Lord, Father. Many hear a creed in them.
b: Verses 4-6 list seven "ones": body, Spirit, hope, Lord, faith, baptism, God. They are often read in three groups that follow the pattern Spirit (4:4), Lord (4:5), Father (4:6), which later Christians took as a sign of the Trinity. The structure also echoes the Jewish confession of the one God, the Shema: "The LORD is our God. The LORD is one" (Deuteronomy 6:4). Paul used the same logic in Romans 3:29-30: because God is one, he is God of Jews and Gentiles alike. Some scholars think Paul is quoting a fixed formula from early worship; the language is hymn-like, but no source for it is known.

t: One baptism: what it is and how it is done
p: Christians agree there is one baptism but differ on what it is, who may receive it and how.
b: Paul takes it for granted that every reader was baptized and that this made them one. He does not say whether he means water baptism, baptism in the Spirit, or both together, and he does not say how it was done or on whom. Churches have drawn different lessons from "one": the older churches refuse to repeat baptism, while some groups reject outward water baptism altogether. See the card for how the traditions differ, and Romans 6:3-4 for Paul's longer teaching. The card is a sample of the traditions, not a full list; Methodist, Churches of Christ and Pentecostal churches, among others, have their own teaching.

p: The Greek for "all" can be "all people" or "all things." Both fit the verse.
b: Greek pas in these three phrases can be masculine (all people, all believers) or neuter (all things, the whole creation). The next verses speak of the church, and "in all" is often read as "in all believers." But "over all" and "through all" read well of creation, and the letter's vision is cosmic (1:10; 4:10). Paul may leave both senses open. The Textus Receptus adds "you" at the end ("in you all"), and the Byzantine text reads "in us all"; see the variant.
orig: ἐπὶ πάντων καὶ διὰ πάντων καὶ ἐν πᾶσιν

a: Each one of us was given grace
p: "Grace" here means the particular gifts Christ gives each person, not the saving favor of 2:8.
b: Here charis is God's gift for service to each believer, as in Romans 12:3, 6 and 1 Corinthians 12:4-11. It is not the saving grace of 2:5, 8 but the favor that equips. The "measure" is Christ's to give, so no one can brag about what they have or despise others for what they lack. The next verse proves the point with a Psalm.

a: he led a crowd of captives, and he gave gifts to people
p: Paul quotes Psalm 68:18 but says "gave" where the Psalm says "took." Jewish readers noticed a similar change.
b: The site's Plain of Psalm 68:18 reads: "You went up on high; you led captives away. You took gifts among humans, even among rebels, so that the LORD God might live there." Paul has "gave" for "took." Reasons offered: (1) a conqueror takes spoil and then hands it out to his people, so both verbs describe one event; (2) the Aramaic Targum of the Psalms addresses Moses, who ascended to the firmament, captured captives, taught Torah and gave gifts to humans, and the Syriac Peshitta reads "gave" (Greever, Tyndale Bulletin 2020; the Targum was written down after Ephesians, and its date relative to Paul is debated); (3) Paul is making his own application. The Psalm celebrates God's march up to Zion; Paul says Christ is that victor. Compare 1:20-22, where the powers are put under Christ's feet.

a: into the lower parts of the earth
p: "The lower parts of the earth" has been read as the realm of the dead, the earth itself, or the regions lower than the earth.
b: Three readings are common, and they differ mostly on how the Greek genitive "of the earth" is taken. (1) The realm of the dead. "The lower parts" are the parts of the earth that lie beneath, the underworld. The Septuagint has related phrases for the place of the dead: Psalm 62:10 (English 63:9) says "into the lowest parts of the earth" (katotata, a superlative; Ephesians has the comparative katotera), and in Ezekiel 32:18 the Greek has a phrase meaning the depth of the earth (Swete's text of the Septuagint). Irenaeus (Against Heresies 5.31.1) read this verse as Christ going where the dead are. (2) The earth itself. "Of the earth" explains "lower": he came down to this earth, in the incarnation. This is a common modern reading. (3) The regions lower than the earth. The genitive is one of comparison, so that the phrase means the places beneath the earth, which again points to the realm of the dead. Commentators weigh all three, and the NET Bible's note takes the second. The word for "parts" is missing in some witnesses (see the variant at this verse), which would leave "the lower [places] of the earth" without settling which of the three is meant. Passages cited for the first reading are 1 Peter 3:19 and Matthew 12:40. See the card.
r: Psalm 63:9; Ezekiel 32:18; Matthew 12:40; Acts 2:27; 1 Peter 3:19; Romans 10:7

a: so that he might fill everything
p: Christ goes down and up so that he can fill everything. The word links to 1:23.
b: The verb "fill" (pleroo) belongs to the letter's fullness language: the church is the fullness of the one who fills everything in every way (see 1:23), and believers are to be filled with all God's fullness (3:19). Here the ascent is not an escape from the world but a way of reaching all of it. The "heavens" are plural, as in Jewish pictures of layers of heaven; Hebrews 4:14 says he passed through them.

p: Paul lists apostles, prophets, evangelists, and "shepherds and teachers." The last two share one article in Greek.
b: These are people given to the church, not boxes on a chart. "Apostles" and "prophets" also appear in 2:20 and 3:5, where they are tied to the church's beginning (see those verses). "Evangelists" are bearers of the good news (Acts 21:8; 2 Timothy 4:5). In Greek one article governs "shepherds and teachers," which ties them closely: either two names for one kind of leader (a teaching shepherd) or two overlapping groups. Whether apostles and prophets continue today is one of the church's old disputes; see the card.
r: Ephesians 2:20; Ephesians 3:5; 1 Corinthians 12:28; Acts 21:8; 2 Timothy 4:5; 1 Peter 5:2

t: Equipping, and who does the work
p: The Greek for "get ready" can mean "mend" or "put in order." Who does the "work of service" is the question.
b: Katartismos comes from a verb used for mending fishing nets (Matthew 4:21) and setting a bone: putting something into working order. Three phrases follow, each with its own preposition: for readying the saints, for the work of service, for building the body. The KJV puts commas between them, so that leaders do all three. Most modern versions read them as a chain: leaders ready the saints, the saints do the work of service, and the body is built up. The Greek can carry either, and the Plain keeps the three "for" phrases as they stand. The chain reading is a central text for the idea that all believers share in ministry.

p: "Full-grown person" is singular. It may mean the church as one body, or each believer's growth.
b: The singular "person" (aner, an adult) is set against the "babies" of 4:14. Many take it of the whole church growing up together into Christ, in line with the "one body" of 4:4 and the "one new humanity" of 2:15. Others see each believer's maturity. "Height" (helikia) can mean stature or age, and "the fullness of Christ" is Paul's language for a goal beyond the believer's own effort. The goal is Christ himself, not an ideal of Christian behavior.

p: The Greek word comes from "dice": gambling, and especially cheating at dice.
b: Kybeia comes from kybos, a die. It was used of gambling and of the trickery that goes with it. The picture is of a teacher who plays with people's lives as a cheat plays a game. The next phrase repeats the idea with "craftiness" and "scheming" (methodeia), the same word that appears in "the schemes of the devil" in 6:11. Paul sees false teaching as part of a larger opposition, not as mere error.

p: Paul's verb is "to truth." Most versions say "speaking the truth," but it can mean living truthfully.
b: The Greek is a single verb, aletheuo, "to be true" or "to act truly." In Galatians 4:16 it is usually rendered "telling the truth," which is why the KJV and many others have "speaking the truth in love." But the verb is wider than speech, and the context (4:14 on false teaching; 4:25 on honest words) supports a double sense: be honest, and live honestly, all within love. The goal is growth "into him," the head, so the body does not grow on its own. The same "head" appears in 1:22; see also the note at 5:23.

a: As each single part does its work in its own measure
p: Paul's picture of the body is also in Romans 12 and 1 Corinthians 12.
b: Romans 12:4 uses the same picture: "A single body has many parts, and the parts do not all have the same work to do." In 1 Corinthians 12 the body shows the need for every member. Ephesians adds two things: the body is held together by a supply that flows "from him" (the head), and the body "builds itself up in love." The Greek "joint" (haphe) means whatever touches and connects. Roman readers knew the picture from political speech: the fable of the body's parts quarreling with the belly was told to calm the city (Livy, History of Rome 2.32).

t: Gentiles told not to live like Gentiles
p: The readers are mostly Gentiles, yet Paul speaks of "the Gentiles" as others. Jews had long spoken this way.
b: 2:11 and 3:1 show that the readers are mostly Gentile by birth, so Paul is telling Gentiles not to live the way other Gentiles live. The list that follows is the standard Jewish criticism of pagan life, found in Wisdom of Solomon 13-14 and in Romans 1:18-32: ignorance of God, idolatry, and sexual excess. The Byzantine text and the Textus Receptus say "the rest of the Gentiles" (the KJV's "other Gentiles"); the older text does not. Without "the rest," "the Gentiles" are the outside world and the readers, though Gentile by birth, are set against it, a thought the letter has developed in 2:11-22. See the variant.
r: Ephesians 2:11; Ephesians 3:1; Romans 1:18; Wisdom of Solomon 14:12; 1 Thessalonians 4:5; 1 Peter 4:3

p: "Futility" (mataiotes) is the word for what is empty and without result, and is used of idols.
b: Mataiotes is the Septuagint's regular word for the Hebrew hevel, the "vapor" of Ecclesiastes. It is also used of idols and of worship that leads nowhere (Jeremiah 2:5; Acts 14:15). Paul used it in Romans 1:21 (the cognate verb) and Romans 8:20 for a creation that cannot reach its goal. Here it describes a mind turned away from God, with emptiness as the result and not just a mistake in thinking.

p: The Greek is the "callus" word: a heart that has gone hard like a healed bone or hardened skin.
b: Porosis began as a medical word for a callus, the hard tissue that forms over a broken bone, and then for loss of feeling. The same family of words is used of Israel's hardening in Romans 11:7, 25 and of the Pharisees in Mark 3:5. In Ephesians the cause is not named as God's act: the ignorance is "inside them," and in the next verse they "handed themselves over." Compare Romans 1:24, where God hands them over; Paul holds both sides together.

p: Romans says God handed them over; Ephesians says they handed themselves over.
b: The verb paradidomi is the one used three times in Romans 1: "God handed them over" (Romans 1:24, 26, 28). Here the subject is the people. The verb is also the one used when Christ "handed himself over for us" (5:2) and for the church (5:25). Paul sets the two handings side by side: people hand themselves over to sensuality; Christ hands himself over in love. "Lost all feeling" is a medical word again (apalgeo, to stop feeling pain), like the "hardening" of 4:18. The Latin Vulgate has "despairing" (desperantes, as the text on vulgate.org reads) where the Greek editions on this site have "lost all feeling," which implies a different Greek verb; the Plain follows the Greek text.

a: as the truth is in Jesus
t: "Learned Christ" and "the truth is in Jesus"
p: Christ is the thing taught. And Paul uses the name "Jesus" alone, rare in his letters.
b: "You learned Christ" is an unusual phrase: Christ is not just the teacher but the subject matter. The Greek "heard him" puts Christ in the accusative; Greek often puts a speaker heard directly in the genitive and uses the accusative for hearing about someone, so some take it as "heard about him." Most commentators say Paul means that Christ is heard in the preaching the readers received, so the phrase does not claim they heard him in person. Then Paul names "Jesus" without a title, which he seldom does. Some read it as pointing to the earthly Jesus and his life as the pattern of the truth. The point is that the "truth" is not a theory but a person whose life shows what the new self looks like.

t: Clothes to take off and put on
p: "Take off" and "put on" are clothing words. In Romans, the old self "was crucified"; here it is taken off.
b: Romans 6:6 says: "our old self was crucified with him," a past event. Ephesians turns it into an instruction: take off the old self, put on the new (4:24). The clothing picture is also in Colossians 3:9-10 and in Galatians 3:27 ("put on Christ"), and many think it echoes the early practice of removing clothes before baptism and putting on a white robe afterward, though no first-century text describes that rite. The "old self" may be the old humanity in Adam (corporate) or the individual's former life; the letter's habit of speaking of one new humanity (2:15) favors both senses together.

a: to be made new in the spirit of your mind
p: "Spirit of your mind" may be the human spirit or the Holy Spirit. Romans 12:2 has the same renewal.
b: Romans 12:2 says: "Be transformed instead, by the renewing of your mind." Here the renewal is "in the spirit of your mind." The phrase is debated: it may mean the mind's inner direction, the believer's spirit, or the Holy Spirit working on the mind. The passive "to be made new" implies that someone else does the renewing, which supports a reference to God or the Spirit at work.

t: The new self and the image
p: The "new self" is described as created like God, which recalls Genesis 1.
b: "Created" (ktizo) is the verb for God's creating, used in 2:10 ("created in Christ Jesus for good works") and 2:15 ("to create in himself one new humanity"). "In line with God" recalls humans made in God's image and likeness in Genesis 1:26-27; Colossians 3:10 says so outright. Where Adam's image was marred, the new self restores it, and the content is given as "righteousness and holiness that truth brings," as against "deceiving desires" in 4:22. See the topic on the image of God.

a: Speak truth, each one of you, with your neighbor
p: Paul quotes Zechariah 8:16, and "neighbor" here means a fellow member.
b: The site's Plain of Zechariah 8:16 reads: "Speak the truth to one another." Paul's wording is close to the Greek Old Testament, which has "Speak truth, each one, to his neighbor"; Paul writes "with" for "to." In the prophet the instruction belongs to the restored Jerusalem, where truth and fair judgment mark the city. Paul turns it on the church: the neighbor is now the fellow believer, "because we are parts of one another," the same phrase as Romans 12:5. The second half of the argument is the body again: lying to a member is a self-injury. Jesus' wider use of "neighbor" (Luke 10:36) is not set aside, but this verse speaks of the community.

a: Be angry, but do not sin
p: Paul quotes Psalm 4 in its Greek form, "Be angry." The Hebrew verb can also mean "tremble."
b: The site's Plain of Psalm 4:4 reads: "Be shaken, but do not sin." The Hebrew verb rigzu means to shake, whether with fear or with anger; the Septuagint chose "be angry," and Paul follows it. Anger itself is not forbidden, but it must not become sin. The Babylonian Talmud reads the Psalm line in another way: a person should stir the good inclination against the evil inclination (Berakhot 5a). "Do not let the sun set on your anger" echoes the rule that a poor worker's wages must be paid before sundown (Deuteronomy 24:15): some wrongs cannot wait. The word for "anger" in the second half (parorgismos) means anger stirred up and nursed.

a: making something good with his own hands
p: The goal of honest work in this verse is not wealth but having something to give to the needy.
b: The verse does not stop at "don't steal" (Exodus 20:15), which the Ten Words already say. The aim of honest work is to share with those in need, an unusual reason in a world where work was often scorned as the business of slaves. Ephesians, like Acts 20:34-35, treats labor as a way to give. The Greek says "working the good" with his own hands, which sets the good work of the hands against the old crooked work of stealing. The text does not say who the thief is. The word "own" (idiais) is absent from the Byzantine text; see the variant.

p: The Greek word is used of spoiled fruit, fish and wood. Words can spoil, too.
b: Sapros means rotten or decayed: fruit gone bad, a rotten tree (Matthew 7:17), a spoiled fish. Many English versions soften it to "unwholesome" or "corrupt." The opposite is speech that builds up, in the same body-building language as 4:12, 16. Speech is the first practical test of 4:25, and Paul gives it a purpose: that it "gives grace" to those who hear.

a: do not cause grief to the Holy Spirit of God
p: Paul's "grieve the Spirit" comes from Isaiah, where Israel did it in the wilderness.
b: The site's Plain of Isaiah 63:10 says: "But they rebelled and grieved his holy spirit." The Hebrew uses "his holy spirit" for God's presence with Israel, and Isaiah says that grieving it turned God into an enemy. The link is to the Hebrew verb ('itstsebu, "grieved"); the Greek Old Testament there says "provoked" (paroxynan), not Paul's word lypeo, so Paul is echoing the idea more than quoting the Greek. Paul, writing to a church, takes the same phrase and says the Spirit can be grieved by sins of speech and temper (4:25-31). That makes the Spirit someone who can feel, not a force. The sealing in 1:13 points to ownership (see that verse). Whether a sealed person can lose that standing is a separate question that the churches answer differently; see the topic on perseverance.

t: Forgive, from the word for grace
p: The Greek verb for "forgive" here is built on the word for grace (charis).
b: The verb is charizomai, which Paul uses elsewhere of forgiving too (2 Corinthians 2:7, 10; Colossians 2:13; 3:13). It is related to charis, "grace," and means to give freely, to forgive as a gift. The comparison is with God's forgiveness "in Christ." Colossians 3:13 says the Lord forgave you. The Byzantine text and the Textus Receptus read "forgave us" where the older manuscripts read "forgave you"; see the variant.

p: "Imitators of God" has a Jewish root: be holy because God is holy. The Gospels give the pattern in Jesus.
b: The Greek mimetes gives English "mimic." The idea is old in Israel: "You will be holy, because I am holy" (Leviticus 19:2). The Talmud asks how a person can follow God and answers with his acts: he clothed the naked, visited the sick, comforted mourners and buried the dead, and so should we (Sotah 14a). Ephesians gives the Christian form: the next verse says the pattern is Christ's love. Paul elsewhere asks readers to imitate himself as he imitates Christ (1 Corinthians 11:1). The phrase "children who are loved" explains why: children copy a father they know loves them.

p: The verb is "hand over." Christ's handing over answers the handing over of 4:19.
b: The verb paradidomi is used for Christ in Galatians 2:20 and Romans 8:32. In Ephesians it matches 4:19, where people "handed themselves over" to sensuality, and it comes back in 5:25 for the church. The verse says "for us," and the manuscripts differ between "us" and "you" (see the variant).

p: Paul uses the Septuagint's phrase for the "soothing smell" of offerings.
b: The Greek osme euodias, "a smell of sweetness," is how the Septuagint renders the Hebrew phrase this site translates "soothing smell," and the Plain uses that same wording here so that the link to the offerings shows. It first appears when Noah offers sacrifice: "The LORD smelled the soothing smell" (Genesis 8:21), and it is the phrase for the burnt offering: "a soothing smell, a gift by fire for the LORD" (Exodus 29:18). Paul says Christ's self-giving was such an offering. He uses the same words of the gift sent by the Philippians (Philippians 4:18). The sacrifice is described in the language of the Temple, though Jesus is neither priest nor animal here; compare Hebrews 9-10.

p: Paul begins a standard list: sexual immorality, impurity, greed. Greed is put in the same list on purpose.
b: Porneia covers sexual conduct outside what the Torah and the early church allowed; the topic page on it shows how its meaning has been debated. The list repeats the one at 4:19, "impurity" and "greed," and Colossians 3:5 has the same three. Putting greed on the list is the point: Paul will say in 5:5 that greed belongs with idolatry. What "not even named" means is rhetoric, not a ban on speaking of sins (Paul names them), but a warning that these should not be at home in the church's talk.

p: Aristotle praised the wit this word names. Paul means a clever, double-edged wit.
b: Eutrapelia is "turning easily," a ready wit. Aristotle names it as a virtue, a quick and graceful humor (Nicomachean Ethics 4.8), and so it was often praised in Greek writing. Paul uses it in a bad sense, probably of joking that cuts, double meanings and sexual wit, in the line with "shameful speech" and "silly talk." It is no argument against humor in general; the opposite he names is thanksgiving, a speech that gives. The Textus Receptus and the Byzantine text change the verb form ("which are not fitting"); this makes no difference in English.

p: One kingdom is shared by Christ and God. Some hear a claim that Christ is God.
b: Greek puts one article before "Christ and God," so the kingdom is a single kingdom. Some commentators read the phrase as calling Christ "God," as in Titus 2:13; others point out that Paul does not call Christ "God" in so many words here and read it as a kingdom both rule together (1 Corinthians 15:24-28). The sentence also states the cost of such lives: those who live this way have no inheritance in it. The churches differ on how a person gets that inheritance and whether it can be lost; see the topic on perseverance.

p: The Greek says greed is idolatry. Later copyists changed the word to say the greedy person is an idolater.
b: The earliest text has a neuter "which" and joins it to "greed": greed is itself idolatry, like treating money as a god. Colossians 3:5 says the same, and Jesus said no one can serve both God and wealth (Matthew 6:24). Later copyists changed "which" to a masculine "who," making the greedy man the idolater (the KJV: "covetous man, who is an idolater"); see the variant. Ephesus, home of Artemis' wealthy temple (Acts 19:24-27), knew how money and religion could blend.

a: God's anger comes on the people who disobey
p: "Sons of disobedience" is a Hebrew way to say people marked by disobedience. The anger is God's.
b: "Sons of" followed by a quality means someone marked by it (compare "sons of light" in 5:8). The same phrase is in 2:2. The anger (orge) is God's, and this site's Plain keeps "anger" for it as in Romans 1:18. "Comes" is a present verb: it may mean that the anger is already at work in the consequences of these acts, as in Romans 1:24, or that it is coming at the end (Colossians 3:6; 1 Thessalonians 1:10). Both ideas are held by commentators, and some hold them together.

t: Light and darkness at Qumran and in Ephesians
p: "Children of light" is also the name the Dead Sea community gave itself.
b: Paul says the readers "were" darkness, not that they lived in it. The pairing of light and darkness is common in the Bible, and a close parallel is the Community Rule from Qumran, which divides humanity into "sons of light" and "sons of darkness" and tells of a "walk" in each (Community Rule 3:13-4:26). Ephesians has no such two-camp view of fixed destinies; the move is from darkness to light, and the readers are told to bring the light to the dark, not to keep away from it (5:11). Paul likewise uses "sons of light" in 1 Thessalonians 5:5.

a: show them up for what they are
p: The Greek verb can mean expose, prove wrong, or correct. Each fits.
b: Elencho means to bring to light and so to prove or convict, and then to rebuke or correct. In John 3:20 the works of those who hate the light "will be exposed," and in Matthew 18:15 it is what you do to a brother who has sinned, in private. The English "expose" hints at a public shaming that the verb does not require. Some commentators hold that the "exposing" is by the life of believers shown as light (5:8-9), others that it includes words of rebuke. The following verses explain the effect: what the light shows becomes light itself.

a: whatever is made visible is light
t: Light makes visible, and what is lit becomes light
p: The sentence is hard. It likely says that what is brought into the light becomes light.
b: The Greek verb phaneroumenon can be passive (what is made visible) or middle (what is becoming visible). The reading adopted here is: everything that light exposes is made visible, and whatever is made visible becomes light. That would mean the exposure of sin is not only judgment but conversion: the person who is lit up is lit up. Another reading takes the last phrase to mean that light is whatever makes things visible, a plain truth. Either way the next verse's call to the sleeping to wake sets the hope for the person caught in darkness.
orig: πᾶν γὰρ τὸ φανερούμενον φῶς ἐστιν (pan gar to phaneroumenon phos estin)

a: Wake up, you who sleep! Stand up from among the dead, and Christ will shine on you.
t: A quotation with no known source
p: Paul says "it says," but no book contains these words. They sound like Isaiah and like a baptism song.
b: Paul introduces this as Scripture ("it says"), but the lines are not in any Old Testament book. They echo two Isaiah passages: "Wake up and sing out, you who lie in the dust!" (Isaiah 26:19) and "Rise up and shine, for your light has come" (Isaiah 60:1). Views: (1) a free blend of those verses; (2) a line from an early Christian hymn or baptism liturgy, a view held by many scholars because of its rhythm and the themes of waking, rising and light; (3) a saying from a lost book. The "dead" and the "sleeping" are those in darkness (5:8), called up into the light.

p: The KJV's "redeeming the time" comes from a Greek market word: to buy up an opportunity.
b: Exagorazo is to buy out of the market, and kairos is the right moment, not clock time. The phrase "buying up the time" also appears in the Greek Daniel 2:8, where the king says the wise men are trying to gain time. Paul means: do not let the chance slip; spend your days on what matters, because "the days are evil," a time of danger and temptation. See the note on "the evil day" at 6:13.

a: do not be drunk with wine
p: Drunkenness and ecstatic worship were linked in Asia Minor. Paul puts the Spirit in place of wine.
b: The command may reflect the cult of Dionysus, the god of wine, widely worshiped in Asia Minor, where drunkenness was part of religious ecstasy (some commentators make the link; it is not proved). The Bible warns against drunkenness (Proverbs 23:31; Luke 21:34) without forbidding wine itself (Psalm 104:15). The same contrast appears at Pentecost, where the disciples were accused of being full of new wine (Acts 2:13-15), and in Luke 1:15. "Reckless living" renders asotia, a word for a wasted life, as of the prodigal son (Luke 15:13, "wasting"). See the card on wine.

t: Filled with, by or in the Spirit?
p: "Be filled" is plural, passive, and in a tense that suggests repetition. The preposition "in" has several senses.
b: The command is to all, in the plural, and the verb is passive: something done to you. The present tense suggests a continuing filling, not a once-for-all event, though Greek tenses do not decide the matter. "In the Spirit" may mean the sphere in which one is filled (the Spirit's presence), the means (by the Spirit's power) or the content (with the Spirit). Churches differ on how this filling relates to baptism and the Spirit's gift at conversion (1:13; 1 Corinthians 12:13); see the card. The next verses show the effects: speech, song, thanks, mutual submission.

a: psalms, hymns and songs from the Spirit
p: Three kinds of song are named. Colossians 3:16 lists the same three.
b: Psalms most likely means the book of Psalms; "hymns" may include Christ hymns such as Philippians 2:6-11 and perhaps 5:14; "songs from the Spirit" may be spontaneous song. Many think the three words overlap rather than being three strict kinds. "Making music" (psallo) first meant plucking a string. Whether that language allows instruments in worship has been argued since the early church; the line "in your heart" is read by some to mean that the music is inward, and by others to describe the spirit in which any music is made. See the card on music in worship.
orig: ψαλμοῖς, ὕμνοις, ᾠδαῖς πνευματικαῖς (psalmois, hymnois, odais pneumatikais)

p: 5:21 is a participle that depends on "be filled," and it introduces the household instructions that follow.
b: The Greek has no break between 5:18 and 5:21: be filled with the Spirit, speaking, singing, giving thanks, submitting. The five participles are the marks of a Spirit-filled community. "To one another" is the point commentators debate. Some hold it means mutual submission among all believers, with the household instructions showing how it looks in different roles. Others say "one another" here means "some to others," the order of the household being the way the submission is given. The verb hypotasso means to arrange oneself under. It is not the word for obey (hypakouo), which Paul uses for children and slaves in 6:1, 5. See the card on headship.

p: Lists of household duties were common in ancient writing. Ephesians adopts the form but changes it.
b: Aristotle's Politics (1.1253b) treats the household as three relations: master and slave, husband and wife, father and children. Josephus, Against Apion 2.201, says the Torah calls the woman inferior and tells her to be subject to her husband. Similar lists are found in Stoic and Jewish writing, and in the New Testament: Colossians 3:18-4:1, 1 Peter 2:18-3:7, Titus 2:1-10. Scholars explain the form in different ways: Martin Dibelius stressed the influence of Stoicism on such codes, and David Balch argued that Ephesians and Colossians follow Aristotle's pattern and that Jewish writers such as Philo and Josephus used such codes to show respect for Roman social order. Ephesians differs by addressing wives, children and slaves directly, as full members who hear the letter read, and by giving each duty a reason "in the Lord." Husbands, fathers and masters are given duties as well.

p: The earliest text has no verb in 5:22. The Plain leaves the verb out too, so that the sentence still hangs on "submitting" in 5:21.
b: In the earliest manuscripts 5:22 reads, "Wives, to your own husbands, as to the Lord," and takes its verb from 5:21 (see the variant). The Plain keeps that shape on purpose, and 5:23 begins with "because," as the Greek does. The later manuscripts that add "submit" read the verse as a command that stands by itself; the earlier text makes the instruction to wives one case of the "submitting to one another" of 5:21. Wives are addressed directly, as responsible persons, unlike household manuals that speak only to the head of the house. "Own" (idios) points to the one husband and marks the limit of the duty. "As to the Lord" gives the reason and the spirit. 1 Peter 3:1-6 and Titus 2:5 say much the same, and Colossians 3:18 adds "as was fitting in the Lord." The meaning of submission is the central dispute; see the card.
orig: Αἱ γυναῖκες τοῖς ἰδίοις ἀνδράσιν (hai gynaikes tois idiois andrasin); the Byzantine text adds ὑποτάσσεσθε (hypotassesthe)

p: "Head" could mean authority, source, or prominence. Scholars have argued about it for decades.
b: Kephale in Greek is the part of the body; the question is its figurative sense. Three main views: (1) authority over, as the head of a household or army (Grudem's 1985 survey of 2,336 examples found no convincing case of "source" and 49 texts where the word means a person of superior rank or a ruler; the Hebrew ro'sh sometimes means chief, as in Judges 11:11); (2) source, like the head of a river, with the body's growth from the head in 4:16 and Christ as the origin of the church (the meaning Grudem's survey tested; he found no convincing example); (3) prominence or preeminence, a leading part (Richard Cervin's 1989 article, titled a rebuttal of Grudem, disputed his conclusion; one survey of the debate, on theologyintheraw.com, groups Cervin with this view). Ephesians adds its own context: God "gave him to the church as head over all things" (1:22), Christ is the head from whom the body grows (4:15-16), and here he is "Savior of the body." The comparison is limited: only Christ is Savior. See the cards on headship and sacrament.
r: Ephesians 1:22; Ephesians 4:15; Ephesians 4:16; 1 Corinthians 11:3; Colossians 1:18; Judges 11:11

p: The phrase raises a question every tradition has had to answer: what are the limits?
b: The phrase says submission reaches every area, but the example is Christ, who gives himself for the church (5:25). Christian teachers have always set limits. Acts 5:29, "Obeying God has to come before obeying people," applies in the home too, and nearly every church statement says submission never means joining in sin. Complementarian writers describe it as willing deference to a husband's leadership; egalitarian writers read 5:21 as the rule and 5:22-24 as one application of it. Many agree that abuse is no part of the picture, and that the husband's calling in 5:25-29 sets his own limits. The card lays out the views.

t: A command no household code gave
p: Ancient lists told husbands to rule well. Ephesians tells them to love, as Christ gave himself.
b: Paul tells husbands to love their wives, and sets the pattern: the self-giving love of Christ, "handing himself over" (compare Galatians 2:20; Ephesians 5:2). Aristotle classed the friendship of husband and wife among friendships between unequals (Nicomachean Ethics 8.7). In a world where the husband's authority was legal and assumed, the demand was for the husband to place himself under the standard of the cross.

a: washing of water, with the spoken word
p: The bath and the word are read as baptism, as the gospel, or both. Wedding baths may lie behind the picture.
b: Ezekiel 16:9 pictures God bathing his bride: "I washed you with water." Paul speaks of the church as the bride. The "washing" (loutron) is read as baptism (Titus 3:5 calls baptism a "washing" of new birth). "The spoken word" (rhema) could be the words said at baptism (the confession of Jesus' name, Acts 22:16), or the gospel message (Romans 10:17). Augustine said the word added to the water makes the sacrament (Tractates on John 80.3). Others take the washing as the inner cleansing of the gospel, to which baptism points. See the card on baptism at 4:5.
orig: τῷ λουτρῷ τοῦ ὕδατος ἐν ῥήματι (to loutro tou hydatos en rhemati)
r: Ezekiel 16:9; Titus 3:5; Acts 22:16; Romans 10:17; 1 Corinthians 6:11; John 15:3

p: The Old Testament pictures Israel as God's bride, and the church takes her place.
b: The prophets often speak of God as the husband of his people: "For your husband is your Maker; the LORD of Armies is his name" (Isaiah 54:5); "I will betroth you to myself forever" (Hosea 2:19). Ephesians gives Christ the part of the husband and the church the part of the bride, and the church is made ready for a wedding day (compare Revelation 19:7-8; 21:2). The words "holy and without fault" echo the language of sacrifices that must be "flawless," and recall 1:4. Some read this as the church's final state; others as what Christ is already doing.
r: Isaiah 54:5; Hosea 2:19; Ezekiel 16:8; 2 Corinthians 11:2; Revelation 19:7; Ephesians 1:4

t: Wife as body, wife as self
p: The husband is to love his wife "as his own body," a thought rooted in Genesis 2.
b: The comparison stands on Genesis 2:23, "bone from my bones and flesh from my flesh," and 2:24, "they become one flesh," which Paul quotes at 5:31. The husband and wife are one body, and so a man who loves his wife is not doing her a favor outside himself. The parallel with the church is that Christ and the church are likewise one body. Paul does not say that wives are the husband's body in a ruling sense; the verse is about care.

p: In Paul "flesh" often means human nature turned against God. Here it means only the body.
b: This site renders sarx as "flesh" everywhere. In Romans 8 it names human nature under sin's power. Here it is neutral, even good: a person's flesh is something he feeds and warms. The context is Genesis 2:24's "one flesh" (5:31). The verb "keeps it warm" (thalpo) is used of a nurse who cherishes her own children (1 Thessalonians 2:7). The Textus Receptus and Byzantine text read "the Lord" for "Christ"; see the variant.

a: and the two will be one flesh
p: Paul quotes Genesis 2:24 from the Greek Old Testament, which has "the two."
b: The site's Plain of Genesis 2:24 reads: "So a man leaves his father and his mother and sticks close to his wife, and they become one flesh." Paul follows the Septuagint's wording, which says "the two will be one flesh"; the Masoretic Text has only "they." The Samaritan Pentateuch also has "the two of them" (Hebrew mishneihem). Jesus quotes the verse in Matthew 19:5 and Mark 10:7-8, and Paul in 1 Corinthians 6:16. Paul's opening words, "because of this," differ from the Septuagint's and from Matthew 19:5. The Byzantine text adds "his" after "father" ("his father and mother"), and the editions differ over whether the Greek says "joined to the wife" with the dative, as the Septuagint does (SBLGNT, Tregelles), or with pros and the accusative (NA28, Tyndale House, Westcott-Hort, Textus Receptus, Byzantine text); see the variant.

a: This mystery is a great one
p: "Mystery" is what God has hidden and now shows. The Latin Bible translated it "sacrament."
b: The mystery in the letter is God's secret plan now made known (1:9; 3:3-9; 6:19). Here the mystery is that the one-flesh union of Genesis 2:24 points to the union of Christ and the church. The Latin Vulgate translated mysterion as sacramentum, "This is a great sacrament," and the verse is one of those cited for the Catholic teaching that marriage is a sacrament (the Council of Trent, session 24, canon 1, defends that teaching). Luther argued that the Latin word misled and that marriage is not a sacrament in the sense of baptism or communion. See the card.
orig: τὸ μυστήριον τοῦτο μέγα ἐστίν (to mysterion touto mega estin)
r: Ephesians 1:9; Ephesians 3:3; Ephesians 3:9; Ephesians 6:19; Genesis 2:24; Romans 11:25

a: I am speaking about Christ and about the church
p: Paul reads Genesis 2:24 as being about Christ and the church. Marriage is the picture, or the picture is marriage.
b: Two directions are possible. One: marriage was designed from the start as a picture of Christ and the church, and Paul uncovers it. The other: Paul takes Christ's love for the church as the pattern for marriage, which is the use he puts it to in 5:25-33. Both can be held together. Typology (a person or event in the Old Testament that foreshadows Christ) is one name for the first. Jewish readers had long read the Song of Songs as a love poem of God and Israel, and some Christian readers read the Song the same way about Christ and the church.
r: Genesis 2:24; Song of Songs 4:7; Hosea 2:19; Ephesians 5:25; Revelation 21:2

p: The Greek verb is "fear," used just before of Christ in 5:21. Most versions say "respect."
b: Phobeo is "to fear." In 5:21 the noun is used of reverence toward Christ, and in the Old Testament "fear" often means awe and respect. Most English versions say "respect" here, and the Plain follows. Paul's shift from "you husbands" (plural) to "each one of you" and then to "the wife" (singular) turns the teaching into a personal duty.

p: Children are addressed directly, which shows they were present when the letter was read.
b: Greek household manuals spoke to the head of the house about his children. Ephesians speaks to the children themselves, which assumes they sat in the gathering and heard the letter read aloud. The verb is "obey" (hypakouo), not the "submit" of 5:21-22, and the limit is "in the Lord" (a phrase some manuscripts omit; see the variant). In Roman law the father held legal power over his household, including his children. Paul's command to children, then, is the family law of the day, with a reason drawn from the Ten Words.

a: Honor your father and your mother
t: The fifth word and its promise
p: Paul quotes the commandment to honor parents and calls it "the first commandment with a promise."
b: The site's Plain of Exodus 20:12 reads: "Honor your father and your mother, so that your days will stretch out long on the land the LORD your God is giving you." Paul's wording is a blend of the two Greek texts. He leaves out "your" after "mother," exactly as the Greek of Exodus 20:12 does (Deuteronomy 5:16 in Greek has it), and his "it will go well with you ... on the earth" matches both; "you will live long" is his own verb form. He drops "the land the LORD your God is giving you," so that a promise about the land of Israel is read as a general one ("the earth"). "First" has been explained as: the first of the Ten Words to carry a promise, since the promise of loyal love in the second word (Exodus 20:6) is a statement about God; or the first in importance. Jewish tradition also counted this commandment as one with a special reward (Mishnah Peah 1:1).

a: do not stir your children to anger
p: In Roman law the father held great power. Paul tells fathers to hold it back.
b: The Roman father (paterfamilias) legally held power over his children, including, in theory, the right of life and death, though the extreme form was seldom used in practice. "Fathers" (pateres) can also mean "parents" (Hebrews 11:23). The command says what a father must not do before what he must do. "Discipline" (paideia) is the training of a child as in Proverbs, where the Hebrew musar is likewise rendered "discipline" on this site; "warning" (nouthesia) is spoken correction. "Of the Lord" means discipline that comes from the Lord and imitates his way.
orig: παιδείᾳ καὶ νουθεσίᾳ κυρίου (paideia kai nouthesia kyriou)

p: Slaves hear the letter as members of the church. They are told to obey, in language that reaches the master too.
b: Slavery was a basic part of Roman life, and household slaves in a city like Ephesus did the work of the house, trades and business. Estimates of how many people were enslaved vary widely; one, by Walter Scheidel, puts it at about 10 percent for the empire as a whole. Slaves could be freed, and many were; many were treated with great cruelty. Ephesians addresses slaves as responsible members of the church, which is itself surprising, and gives their service a new master, "Christ." The letter does not say that slavery should end and does not tell masters to free anyone; Philemon 16, 1 Corinthians 7:21 and Galatians 3:28 are the passages that churches have argued over. See the card, and the chapter page for the longer discussion. The Greek word is doulos, "slave." Many English Bibles say "servant" or "bondservant" here; the word means a person owned by another, and the Plain keeps "slave," as it does for "slaves of Christ" in 6:6.
r: Colossians 3:22; 1 Peter 2:18; Titus 2:9; Philemon 1:16; 1 Corinthians 7:21; Galatians 3:28

p: The Greek says "masters according to the flesh," to set them against the real Master, Christ.
b: The phrase is the same as Colossians 3:22. "According to the flesh" here means in the earthly, human sphere, in contrast to the heavenly Lord who is above them (6:9). It is a limit on the master's claim: he is master of a person's working life, not of the whole person. The word "flesh" here is neutral, as in 5:29. Slaves are to serve "with fear and trembling" (compare Philippians 2:12), and "single-minded" (haplotes) can also mean generous.

t: Same Lord for slave and free
p: Slave and free stand equal before the Lord who will repay both. Galatians 3:28 says the same of the church.
b: The reward is the same for "slave or free," and 6:9 will say the master has the same Lord and no favoritism with him. This echoes Galatians 3:28 ("There is no slave and no free person") and Colossians 3:11, and it sets a limit on the social order without abolishing it. In the church's worship, the enslaved and the free stood together. Some readers point to this as the seed of later abolition; others point out that the letter itself does not give the command to free anyone. Both are true of the text.

p: The Greek uses one word for "masters" and "Lord." The wordplay is lost unless the reader is told.
b: The word kyrios means both "master" of a household and "Lord." In 6:5 and 6:9 the "masters" are kyrioi; here Paul says that the kyrios of both is in heaven. The Plain uses "Lord" for Christ and "masters" for the human ones, so the repeated Greek word is hidden. It is a reversal: the one who has a master-slave relation is himself a slave of a higher Lord. Compare 1 Corinthians 7:22.

p: The Greek word means "lifting of the face," a Hebrew idiom for taking someone's side because of status.
b: The Greek prosopolempsia is built on the Hebrew idiom nasa panim, "lift the face," to favor a person for rank or looks. The Torah says of God that "He does not play favorites, and he does not take a bribe" (Deuteronomy 10:17). Paul uses it in Romans 2:11 for God's judgment of Jew and Gentile, and here for master and slave. The point is not that rank vanishes, but that rank buys no advantage in God's judgment.

p: The strength vocabulary of 1:19 returns here: power, strength, might.
b: Paul piles up three words for strength, as in 1:19. The verb "be made strong" is passive, so the power is God's gift, not the believer's own. "Finally" is literally "from now on" in the oldest text, and in the Byzantine text "finally, my brothers" (see the variant). The command is the start of a new unit: the church as an army in the field, equipped by God.

p: The armor belongs to God. In Isaiah and the Wisdom of Solomon he wears it, and here he lends it.
b: Isaiah 59:17 pictures God as a warrior: "Righteousness he wore as his armor, with salvation as a helmet on his head." Isaiah 11:5 gives the Messiah "righteousness as the band around his waist." The Wisdom of Solomon, a Greek-Jewish book that Catholic and Orthodox churches count as Scripture, describes God taking zeal as armor, righteousness as a breastplate, and impartial judgment as a helmet (Wisdom of Solomon 5:17-20). Paul gives the armor to the church. The Greek panoplia is the full soldier's kit. A Roman guard stood by Paul in custody (Acts 28:16), and 1 Thessalonians 5:8 had already named a breastplate of faith and love and a helmet of hope. See the card on spiritual warfare.
r: Isaiah 59:17; Isaiah 11:5; Wisdom of Solomon 5:17; 1 Thessalonians 5:8; Romans 13:12; Acts 28:16

p: The Greek word for "schemes" is the one used for the "scheming" of false teaching in 4:14.
b: Methodeia, a planned method of getting something done, appears here and at 4:14, the only two times in the New Testament. Paul sees error as a method, and behind it a mind. The word for "devil" (diabolos, "slanderer") was already used at 4:27. "Stand" is the main verb of the passage and occurs four times (6:11, 13, 14); the armor is for holding ground.

p: Paul's word is wrestling: close, hand to hand, not a distant battle.
b: Pale is the Greek word for a wrestling bout, a contest in which the opponent grips you. Ephesus had athletic games, and Paul uses sports images elsewhere (1 Corinthians 9:24-27). "Blood and flesh" is the common Jewish expression "flesh and blood" with the words reversed, meaning mere humans. The point is not that humans are harmless, but that the real struggle is with powers behind them.

a: against the rulers, against the authorities
p: Four names for powers; two of them also appear in 1:21 and 3:10.
b: The names "rulers" (archai) and "authorities" (exousiai) are in 1:21 and 3:10 (see those verses), and "world-rulers" (kosmokratores) occurs nowhere else in the New Testament. Jewish background: each nation had its angelic "prince" (Daniel 10:13, 20), tied to Deuteronomy 32:8's "sons of God" in the Greek text, and 1 Enoch and Jubilees (Ethiopian Orthodox Scripture, in no other church's Bible) developed this. The Community Rule and the War Scroll from Qumran describe angelic and demonic armies. Ephesus was famed for magic (Acts 19:19). The Catholic Catechism (391, 395) and Calvin (Institutes 1.14.13-19) agree that the devil was created good and fell, and that his power is real but limited by God. Readings: personal spiritual beings (the church's traditional view); the spirit of institutions and structures; and a mythic way of speaking of evil that modern readers should translate.
r: Ephesians 1:21; Ephesians 3:10; Daniel 10:13; Deuteronomy 32:8; Colossians 2:15; Acts 19:19

p: Here it is where the evil powers are; in 2:6 it is where believers are seated.
b: Ephesians uses "the heavenly places" (en tois epouraniois) in 1:3, 1:20, 2:6, 3:10 and here. It is the realm of God's presence and Christ's rule, where believers are already seated with him (2:6), yet here also the home of evil spiritual forces. The Plain's "heavenly world" keeps the phrase wide. Readers have taken it as the air or lower heavens (2:2 speaks of a ruler of the air), or as the unseen order of reality, where the spiritual conflict happens beside the visible one.

p: "The evil day" may mean any time of crisis, the present age, or the final battle.
b: In 5:16 "the days are evil," and here there is one "evil day." Readings: (1) any day of attack and temptation; (2) the whole present age, which the powers dominate; (3) the final day of tribulation before the end (compare Amos 5:18 on the day of the LORD). The Greek verb translated "done everything" (katergazomai) can also mean "overcome everything"; most take the first. The result is the same: the soldier is still on his feet.

p: The belt held the soldier's gear together. Truth and righteousness are the first two pieces.
b: The belt of a Roman soldier held up his tunic and carried his sword; tightening it meant getting ready for action. Isaiah 11:5 gives the Messiah a belt of righteousness and faithfulness. The breastplate guarded the chest and heart. Josephus describes the Roman infantry as armed with breastplates and helmets, with swords on both sides (Jewish War 3.93; 3.5.5 in Whiston's numbering). Commentators disagree whether "truth" is the truth of the gospel or honesty of life, and whether "righteousness" is God's gift or the believer's upright conduct; the passage's debt to Isaiah, where righteousness is God's own, supports the first in each pair.

a: the readiness of the good news of peace
p: "Readiness" has three senses: eagerness to tell, a firm footing, or readiness given by the news.
b: The Roman soldier's boots had studs for grip. The Greek word hetoimasia means readiness or preparation, and the genitive "of the good news" is open: (1) readiness to proclaim the good news; (2) the firm footing the good news gives; (3) a readiness that comes from it. The phrase also echoes Isaiah 52:7: "How lovely on the mountains are the feet of the one who brings good news, who makes peace heard." Paul has used the same verse in 2:17 (see that verse), where Christ proclaimed peace. "Peace" is the letter's theme from 2:14.

p: The large Roman shield stopped fire arrows. The "evil one" fires burning missiles.
b: The Greek thyreos is the large door-shaped shield that covered a soldier's body, not the small round one. Ancient armies shot arrows wrapped in burning material, and these shields could take them. Paul's picture is of attacks, perhaps temptation, accusation, doubt or persecution, that faith puts out. "Faith" here is trust in God, not the content of belief. The "evil one" (ho poneros) is the devil himself (6:11), as in Matthew 6:13 and 1 John 2:13.

p: The sword is the one weapon for attack. "The word" can be Scripture, the gospel, or a word the Spirit gives.
b: The Greek is rhema, a spoken word, and not logos. Views: (1) the Bible, as in Jesus' use of Scripture against the devil (Matthew 4:1-11); (2) the gospel message (Romans 10:17); (3) the word given in the moment by the Spirit (Mark 13:11; Ephesians 6:19). Isaiah 11:4 says the Messiah's mouth "will be a rod to strike the earth," and Isaiah 49:2 says, "He made my mouth a sharp sword." Hebrews 4:12 and Revelation 1:16 describe the word as a sword.
r: Isaiah 11:4; Isaiah 49:2; Hebrews 4:12; Revelation 1:16; Matthew 4:4; Mark 13:11

p: Prayer is not a seventh piece of armor but the way all of it is used.
b: The list of weapons has no verb of its own for prayer: it is a participle ("praying") tied to "stand." The word "every" is used four times in the Greek: every kind of prayer, every moment, all persistence, all the saints. "In the Spirit" ties to 2:18, where Jew and Gentile have access to the Father "in one Spirit," and to Romans 8:26-27. "Stay alert" is literally "stay awake," and Jesus used it in Gethsemane (Mark 14:38). The prayer is "for all the saints," meaning all believers, living members of the church.

p: Paul, in chains, asks for prayer to speak freely. The "mystery" here is the good news itself.
b: The "mystery" is the subject of chapter 3: Gentiles share in the promise through the good news (3:3-9). Paul does not ask for his release but for "a word" and for "freedom and courage" (parresia) to speak. A similar request, with the same word for freedom and courage, is in Acts 4:29-31, where the believers pray under threat and the building shakes. It is also in Colossians 4:3-4, where he asks for "an open door."

p: An ambassador was protected by law. Paul is one, in chains.
b: Presbeuo means to serve as an envoy, the word for a representative of an emperor or king. Ambassadors were meant to be inviolable, so "in a chain" is a paradox: the king's envoy is a prisoner. 2 Corinthians 5:20 uses the verb in the plural for all who preach, and Acts 28:20 has Paul say, "This chain is around me on account of Israel's hope." The singular "chain" fits the Roman practice of chaining a prisoner to his guard, as in Acts 28:16.

t: Tychicus, and the copy of Colossians
p: Tychicus carries the letter. The words about him are almost the same as in Colossians.
b: Tychicus was from Asia (Acts 20:4: "from Asia, Tychicus and Trophimus") and is named in Colossians 4:7, 2 Timothy 4:12 and Titus 3:12. Ephesians 6:21-22 repeats Colossians 4:7-8 almost word for word, a run of about thirty Greek words. Views differ on what this shows. Some hold that Paul, or a secretary, wrote both letters at the same time and sent them with Tychicus. Others hold that a later writer copied Colossians to give his letter a personal touch. A messenger like Tychicus normally explained and added to the letter in person. The "faithful servant" is diakonos, the word behind "deacon" (Romans 16:1).

p: The Greek is the plural "brothers," used of a mixed group. The Plain keeps it, as in Romans and Acts.
b: The Greek adelphoi is the masculine plural, and Greek used it for a mixed group; Paul means all the believers, women and men. This site renders it "brothers" in Romans and Acts, and the Plain follows. See the note at Romans 1:13. The wish for "peace" echoes the Jewish blessing shalom. The closing has no personal greetings, an absence that has been taken as a sign that the letter was meant for more than one church (see the book page).

p: The Greek is "in incorruptibility." It may describe the love, the grace, or the Lord.
b: The last words are en aphtharsia, "in incorruption." The phrase may go with: (1) love, an undying love (the Plain); (2) grace, grace that is undying; or (3) the Lord Jesus Christ, "our Lord Jesus Christ in incorruption." The word elsewhere in Paul is the quality of the resurrection body (1 Corinthians 15:42, 50, 53). The prayer for grace "with all who love" reaches past the readers to every believer, which suits a letter that may have gone to several churches. The Textus Receptus and Byzantine text add "Amen," and some copies a note "written from Rome" that is not part of the letter; see the variant.
